name: Chemical reconstruction of skin scars

card.summary: Spot-applying strong TCA acid into individual acne scars; studied in small trials.
card.note: Clinician procedure; sources found are thin.

quick.overview:
CROSS places a strong TCA solution into individual depressed scars, mainly acne scars, instead of peeling the whole face.

Only small trial registrations were found in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: The acid is said to trigger a focal wound-healing response in the scar base.
quick.risks: TCA peels can cause redness, pigment change and scarring. The technique is performed by clinicians.

lead: Chemical reconstruction of skin scars (CROSS) is a dermatology technique for making deep, narrow acne scars, especially ice-pick scars, look shallower so the skin surface reads smoother and more even. Instead of peeling the whole face, a clinician applies a very high-strength trichloroacetic acid (TCA) solution directly into the base of each individual scar [1].

The acid triggers a controlled local injury, and the skin responds by building new collagen that lifts the depressed scar floor toward the surrounding surface. Published reports describe use for acne scars, varicella scars, enlarged pores and depressed surgical scars [1]. Reviews describe it as especially suited to ice-pick scars [1][2].

Published work includes small clinical trials and comparison studies against fractional lasers, and a 2026 review pooled 34 publications covering 937 patients [2]. Many specialists use it alongside other scar treatments such as subcision, microneedling or lasers [2][3].

chain: High-strength TCA applied to the base of an individual atrophic scar
Controlled local injury prompts new collagen formation
Scar floor rises closer to surrounding skin
angle.text: CROSS targets pitted acne scars one by one, so skin texture looks more even without treating the whole face. Practitioners and studies describe it as most useful for ice-pick scars, with several sessions typically involved.

infobox: Ice-pick and some boxcar acne scars; also varicella and surgical scars [1][2]
Focal application with a fine needle, toothpick or brush [2][5]
Dermatologic Therapy, 2008 report of a 50% variant [4]

paras: CROSS applies a high concentration of TCA to the bottom of atrophic scars rather than as a surface peel. Wikipedia describes TCA as a medium-depth peel agent used in office settings and lists acne scars among peel indications; the focal CROSS variant is a more targeted use of the same chemistry [6].

Application tools described in the literature include fine-gauge needles and paintbrush or toothpick-type applicators. One report describes using a 27-gauge tuberculin syringe tip as the applicator [2][5].

A review of 19 articles from 2002 to 2018 found that in studies using a quantitative grading scale for acne scars, 60 to 100 percent of patients showed more than 25 percent improvement, and 83 to 100 percent did in two studies of varicella scars [1].

A 2026 review of 34 publications and 937 patients reported use primarily for ice-pick and boxcar scars, with varying application techniques and adjunct therapies [2]. A 2008 clinical trial evaluated a 50 percent concentration as an alternative to the 90 percent used in earlier work, aiming to reduce local adverse effects [4]. A 2025 randomized trial of 40 patients compared 70 and 100 percent TCA in the CROSS technique [7].

Studies include a randomized trial comparing CO2 laser pinpoint irradiation with CROSS for ice-pick acne scars [8], a split-face trial comparing a 1,550 nm fractional erbium:glass laser with CROSS [9], a trial of 70 percent TCA CROSS [10] and a randomized trial of topical timolol added to TCA-CROSS [11].

A completed registered trial (NCT07028567, 13 participants, started 2023) compares subcision followed by diluted calcium hydroxylapatite injection with subcision followed by painted CROSS TCA for atrophic acne scars; no results were available [12]. A 2024 review of procedural acne scar treatments places chemical approaches among the options [3].

Reported complications are mostly temporary and include post-inflammatory pigment change, redness, pain, itching, infection and widening of scars; it is described as well tolerated in Fitzpatrick skin phototypes I to V [1]. Peels in general can cause prolonged redness, pigment change and scarring [6].

timeline.event: A clinical trial reports a 50% TCA CROSS protocol for grade 3 atrophic acne scars [4].
A comprehensive review compiles 19 CROSS articles and notes no standardized guideline exists [1].
A review of 34 publications and 937 patients examines techniques, adjuncts and complications [2].
